blocks.text: From the earliest days of experimental chemistry, scientists have recognised acids and bases by their distinct properties. Acids taste sour; bases are bitter. Acids and bases also change the colour of certain dyes called indicators, such as litmus and phenolphthalein: acids turn litmus from blue to red and phenolphthalein from pink to colourless, while bases turn litmus from red to blue and phenolphthalein from colourless to pink. As these colour changes show, acids and bases neutralise each other, reacting to produce ionic substances called salts. Acidity in the stomach is due to excess HCl and is treated with mild bases such as baking soda.

In 1923 the Danish chemist J. N. Bronsted and the English chemist T. M. Lowry independently extended the Arrhenius theory, whose limitation is that it describes the reaction of an acid and a base only in aqueous medium, although many reactions occur in other solvents or without any solvent. They pointed out that acid-base reactions can be seen as proton-transfer reactions, so acids and bases can be defined by the transfer of a proton (H+).

blocks.title: Bronsted-Lowry acid and base
blocks.text: According to the Bronsted-Lowry concept, an acid is the species donating a proton in a proton-transfer reaction and a base is the species accepting the proton.

When HCl dissolves in water, a proton is transferred from HCl to water, where it attaches to a lone pair on the O atom and forms H3O+: HCl(g) + H2O(l) gives H3O+(aq) + Cl-(aq). HCl, the proton donor, is the acid and H2O, the proton acceptor, is the base. The species formed after a Bronsted base accepts a proton is called the conjugate acid, so the hydronium ion H3O+ is the conjugate acid of water; the species formed when an acid donates a proton is called the conjugate base. HCl / Cl- and H2O / H3O+ are conjugate acid-base pairs.

When ammonia dissolves in water, proton transfer also occurs: an H+ from H2O attaches to the lone pair of the N atom, forming NH4+ and OH-: NH3(g) + H2O(l) gives NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq). Here H2O (the acid) has donated the proton and NH3 (the base) has accepted it; NH3 / NH4+ and H2O / OH- are the conjugate pairs. These examples show that water is amphoteric, acting as a base in one case and as an acid in the other: an amphoteric substance can act as either an acid or a base (lose or gain a proton) depending on the other reactant. The theory also applies to solvents other than water and to solventless reactions: gaseous ammonia and HCl give solid NH4Cl, HCl donating a proton to NH3, which acts as a base even though no hydroxide ion is present.
